audience_one_line: Someone who has heard the word IPO, maybe seen one in the news, but could not actually explain what it is. They want to genuinely understand it: what happens, why a company does it, what changes afterwards — and then, precisely, how India decides who is allowed to do one.
must_answer: What an IPO IS, in plain words a beginner understands: the first time a company sells its shares to the general public, after which those shares trade on a stock exchange and the company is 'listed'. Lead with this. The reader must be able to define an IPO after the opening paragraph.

WHY a company goes public, explained as the genuinely common-knowledge thing it is (no citation needed): to raise fresh capital for the business, and/or to let early owners — founders, private-equity backers — sell some of their stake and cash out. Make the fresh-issue vs offer-for-sale distinction concrete here.
What changes for the company once it is public: shares trade freely, ownership is dispersed, and it now answers to public-market disclosure. Brief, plain.

Then, and only then, how India polices who is allowed to IPO: the negative list under Regulation 5 (debarred entities, wilful defaulters, fugitive economic offenders, the outstanding-convertibles bar) and the two positive routes under Regulation 6 (the profitability route with its real thresholds, and the compulsory-QIB book-building route for companies that cannot meet them). Ground every threshold and rule with the source.

How an IPO differs from an FPO and an OFS, explained by the simple distinction (is the company already listed? is anyone issuing new shares, or just selling old ones?) before the regulatory definitions.
must_not_say: Investment advice of any kind — whether the reader should apply to IPOs, which are good, how to spot a winner. Reference writing, not tips.
Predictions about which companies will IPO or how 'hot' the market is.
US/UK comparisons unless a sourced excerpt supports the point.
Cliché motivational framing ('an IPO is a coming-of-age milestone', 'a company's dream'). Explain plainly and concretely instead — that is different from being dry and legalistic.
The post-allotment listing-day and allotment mechanics — those live in the Mechanics articles. This piece stops at: what an IPO is, why it happens, and who is allowed to do one.
angle: Teach a beginner what an IPO actually is, then show them how India regulates it. Open with the plain idea — a private company selling shares to the public for the first time, to raise money and/or let early owners cash out, after which it trades on the NSE and BSE. Make it concrete. THEN turn to the part most explainers skip and we get right: SEBI does not let just anyone list. There is a bar — a negative list of who is kept out, and two positive routes in. The article's spine is explain-then-ground: the concept in plain language first, the regulation as the precise proof second. It should read like a brilliant teacher who has also read the actual rulebook, not like the rulebook.
notes: Regenerated after the first attempt came out in legal-memo voice. The corpus already contains the eligibility excerpts (Reg 4 reference date, Reg 5 negative list, Reg 6(1) profitability route, Reg 6(2) compulsory-QIB route, definitions). Coverage is sufficient. The fix is voice + framing: the plain-language explanation of what an IPO is and why companies do it is common knowledge and must be written WITHOUT citation; only the specific eligibility thresholds and named regulations carry source tags. This brief is itself the test of the explain-then-ground prompt changes.
